title: Before You Give Them Another Chance… Read What Jesus Actually Said About Forgiveness, Trust, and Wisdom
paragraphs:
Before You Give Them Another Chance… Read What Jesus Actually Said About Forgiveness, Trust, and Wisdom
Grace does not erase wisdom. Forgiveness is commanded. Reconciliation is conditional. And sometimes the most Christ-like thing you can do is stop enabling the sin that keeps destroying both of you.
There is a pain that almost every person carries but rarely speaks about honestly.
The pain of wondering whether giving someone "one more chance" is actually love... or simply fear of letting go.
Maybe they lied again.
Maybe they betrayed your trust.
Maybe they apologized with tears, only to repeat the same wounds.

Maybe you've spent years convincing yourself that being a "good Christian" means enduring endless cycles of manipulation, abuse, betrayal, or emotional exhaustion because forgiveness means never saying enough.
And every time your heart whispers, "I can't keep doing this," guilt immediately answers, "Jesus said forgive."
But... did He say to keep placing yourself back into the same destruction without wisdom?
That question has quietly imprisoned countless believers.
Not because they don't love Jesus.
But because they've confused forgiveness with permission.
They've confused mercy with enabling.
They've confused grace with the absence of boundaries.
And that confusion has broken families, ministries, friendships, businesses, marriages, and hearts.
The Gospel tells a far deeper story.
It is a story that begins with a scandal.
Not your scandal.
God's.
The holy God welcoming sinners.
The righteous Judge embracing rebels.
The Creator pursuing those who crucified His own Son.
That is why our mission has always been this:
Before we answer whether someone deserves another chance, we must first understand something even bigger.
God Himself is infinitely forgiving.
Yet God never ignores repentance.
That truth alone changes everything.
When Jesus taught His disciples about forgiveness, He never minimized sin.
In Luke 17:3–4, He said:

"Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, 'I repent,' you must forgive him."
The Greek text says:
ἐὰν μετανοήσῃ (ean metanoēsē)

The verb μετανοέω (metanoeō) literally means "to change one's mind," but in biblical usage it carries the deeper meaning of turning away from sin toward God. Repentance is not merely feeling sorry. It is a transformed direction of life.
Biblical forgiveness is never the denial of evil. It is the refusal to seek personal vengeance while entrusting justice to God.
Paul writes in Romans 12:19:
Forgiveness releases revenge.
It does not erase consequences.
This distinction appears throughout Scripture.
King David was forgiven after his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12), yet the consequences remained.
Moses was forgiven, yet he did not enter the Promised Land (Numbers 20).
Peter denied Christ three times, yet Jesus restored him because Peter's heart truly returned to Him (John 21).
Judas felt remorse.
Peter repented.
The Greek language makes this distinction beautifully.
Judas experienced μεταμέλομαι (metamelomai)—regret, sorrow over the outcome.
Peter experienced μετάνοια (metanoia)—true repentance, a changed heart returning to God.
One leads to despair.
The other leads to restoration.
Many people apologize because they were caught.
Far fewer repent because they love holiness.
That difference matters.
Even God Himself does not reconcile with those who refuse repentance.
John 3:36 says:
"Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
Notice something astonishing.
God's love is unconditional.
Relationship with Him is offered freely through grace.
But fellowship is entered through repentance and faith in Christ.
If even God does not ignore rebellion, why do we believe Christians must continually ignore destructive behavior in the name of love?
Jesus certainly didn't.
In Matthew 10:14 He instructed His disciples:
"If anyone will not receive you or listen to your words, shake off the dust from your feet."
That wasn't hatred.
That was wisdom.
In Matthew 7:6 Jesus said:
"Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs..."
These difficult words are not insults; they are vivid Jewish imagery warning against repeatedly entrusting what is sacred to those determined to trample it. Love is never naïve.
Even Jesus Himself did not entrust Himself to everyone.
John 2:24–25 tells us:
"But Jesus on His part did not entrust Himself to them... because He knew what was in man."
The Greek uses the same root verb πιστεύω (pisteuō)—to believe or entrust. The text literally says Jesus "did not entrust Himself" to certain people because He knew their hearts.
Think about that.
Jesus loved everyone.
Jesus died for sinners.
Jesus forgave His enemies.
Yet Jesus did not automatically trust everyone.
Love and trust are not identical.
Forgiveness is freely given.
Trust is faithfully rebuilt.
Grace is a gift.
Trust is earned.
That distinction has rescued countless wounded believers from unnecessary guilt.
Some of you have spent years believing that setting healthy boundaries meant you lacked faith.
But Scripture paints a different picture.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
"Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life."
The Hebrew reads:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ (mikkol mishmar netzor libbekha)

The verb נָצַר (natsar) means to guard, watch over, preserve, or protect carefully. Guarding your heart is not building walls of bitterness; it is exercising God-given stewardship over what He has entrusted to you.
Biblical love never celebrates repeated destruction.
Real love seeks the highest good of another person.
Sometimes that highest good requires confrontation.
Sometimes distance.
Sometimes accountability.
Sometimes consequences.
Hebrews 12 reminds us that God disciplines those He loves.
Love that never confronts sin is not biblical love.
It is sentimental tolerance.
Paul instructed the church to restore sinners "in a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1), but restoration assumes repentance and a willingness to turn back to Christ.
Without repentance, reconciliation becomes impossible because trust cannot grow where truth is continually rejected.
Perhaps this is why so many believers are emotionally exhausted.
They keep reopening wounds that God never commanded them to reopen.
They keep calling enabling "Christian love."
Meanwhile Jesus quietly stands beside them saying,
"My child...
I never told you to become someone's savior.
I already am."
That sentence alone changes everything.
You cannot redeem another person's heart.
Only Christ can.
You cannot manufacture repentance.
Only the Holy Spirit grants genuine conviction (2 Timothy 2:25).
You cannot heal someone determined to keep choosing darkness.
You can pray.
You can forgive.
You can bless.
You can refuse revenge.
But you are not required to participate indefinitely in another person's unrepentant sin.
Sometimes the most loving thing you can do is step back and allow consequences to become the teacher you never could be.
That is not giving up.
That is trusting God enough to let Him work where you cannot.
Perhaps someone reading this has become the person always asking for "one more chance."
If that is you, hear this with hope.
Jesus specializes in rewriting broken stories.
No betrayal is beyond His grace.
No addiction is beyond His power.
No scandal is beyond His redemption.
The Gospel is filled with people who failed spectacularly and were transformed by Christ.
Peter.
Paul.
The Samaritan woman.
Zacchaeus.
The thief on the cross.
Their stories are not about perfect people.
They are about a perfect Savior.
The heartbeat of the Gospel is not that people deserve another chance.
It is that Jesus gives new life to those who truly turn to Him.
That is grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses sin.
But costly grace purchased by the blood of Christ.
The cross never minimizes sin.
It reveals its terrible cost.
The empty tomb never minimizes failure.
It declares that failure does not have the final word when Christ is Lord.
Maybe today you need to forgive someone without reopening the same door.
Maybe today you need to repent instead of merely apologizing.
Maybe today you need to stop trying to save someone who refuses to be saved and instead entrust them to the Savior who never fails.
Wherever you find yourself, remember this:
Jesus never asks you to choose between grace and wisdom.
He calls you to walk in both.
Because that is exactly how He loves us.
Sometimes God uses a shared testimony to begin a conversation that changes a life.
Let God's Word shape your decisions more than your pain or your fear.
If you desire to glorify God through this ministry, your support becomes part of that mission.
Because eternity is too important for shallow faith, and one surrendered heart can become the beginning of another person's salvation story.
